newsitem.title: USA: Missile test plan angers Florida Keys residents.
newsitem.headline: Missile test plan angers Florida Keys residents.

text.p: A U.S. Air Force plan to launch up to 12 target missiles a year over the pristine waters of the Florida Keys is gaining bureaucratic momentum, but local residents are promising to fight back.

"Except at the point of a gun there's no way they're going to make me leave my home. And I'm not going to be sequestered in my home either," said Dennis Henize, who lives less than two miles (three km) from the proposed missile site on Cudjoe Key in the lower keys.

Under the plan, Hera target missiles would blast off just yards (metres) from a public boat ramp and soar over the famed keys back country, a vast uninhabited region of turquoise waters, mangrove islands and deep-green turtle grass. Air Force officials say no one will have to evacuate the area and traffic will not be disrupted on U.S. 1, the only road linking the keys.

The missiles would mimic new Iraqi or North Korean rockets as part of the Clinton administration's plan to improve U.S. defences against shorter range "theater" missiles. The Air Force hopes to knock the rockets down over the Gulf of Mexico with experimental missiles fired from Eglin Air Base in the Florida panhandle. The tests would begin in 1999.

The debris from a launch accident would fall harmlessly within a fan-shaped "hazard zone" that would temporarily be cleared of boat and air traffic during each launch, Air Force Major Tom Kennedy, the missile test manager at Eglin, said.
If the rockets miss each other, their trajectory would carry them harmlessly into the Gulf of Mexico, he said.

Such assurances are hard to sell in the keys, where suspicion of "big government" is rampant. Residents fear the launches could pollute the fragile ecosystem, snarl traffic and destroy their homes in a launch calamity.

Next month the Air Force will begin public reviews required by law before the missile tests can go ahead. The first hearings are scheduled in Key West on Jan. 27, Marathon on Jan. 28 and Tavernier on Jan. 30.

Kennedy said the Air Force was studying the environmental consequences of a launch mishap. Even if the aluminium-based solid fuel and other debris lands in the cordoned-off zone, the keys have strong currents that could disperse the debris widely.
A new missile assembly building and launch pad would have to be built at Cudjoe, which is home to two radar-equipped Air Force blimps dubbed "fat alberts" by locals.

Residents plan to question the Air Force on every point, expecially the distance between the proposed launch pad and the nearest home. For the plan to go ahead, the distance must be at least 6,500 feet (2,000 metres), Kennedy said.
The Air Force plans to visit the island in February to measure the distance precisely.

The missile debate could also become entangled in the thorny debate over the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a 2,600-square-mile (6,700-sq-km) refuge that has been the subject of controversy for six years. Some residents ask how the federal government can restrict their fishing rights in the sanctuary while permitting the Air Force to launch missiles through it.

"I understand the Air Force position but the same federal government has declared this area a national treasure, in essence, a national sanctuary," Keith Douglas, chairman of the Monroe County Commission that represents the Keys, said.

Sanctuary officials are doing their best to steer clear of the controversy. Spokeswoman Alyson Simmons said the missiles would not actually be launched from the sanctuary but from land along its border.
Douglas wants the Air Force to launch the targets from planes, but the Air Force has ruled that out. "The ground launch is the only proven launch method we have just now," Kennedy said.
The United States has other test ranges available but none of them are suitable for these types of tests, he added.
